svg.text: Surveillance: the ward is where an epidemic is first visible
Under IDSR the whole country reports weekly, and DHIS2 is where it lands.
Report these immediately — not weekly, not at the end of the shift
Cholera · Meningitis · Yellow fever · Measles · Viral haemorrhagic fever
Acute flaccid paralysis, for polio · Guinea worm · Neonatal tetanus · Any unusual cluster
A single suspected case is the trigger. You do not wait for laboratory confirmation to notify.
Zero reporting is mandatory: if nothing occurred, you report the nothing. A blank return is not a report.
What you do, in order
1. Treat and isolate the patient
2. Notify upward at once — the DHMT
3. Record the case with a full address
4. Take the specimen the guideline names
5. Trace and follow the contacts
6. Health education, without blame
The three questions of an investigation
PERSON — who is affected? Age, sex, occupation
PLACE — where are they? Map the cases
TIME — when did they start? Draw the curve
Cases clustered around one water source, all
starting within a day or two, point to a single
common exposure rather than spread person to person.
Words examiners use precisely
ENDEMIC — always present in the area, at a fairly steady level. Malaria in most of Ghana.
EPIDEMIC / OUTBREAK — clearly more cases than expected for that place and season.
PANDEMIC — an epidemic crossing countries and continents.
SPORADIC — scattered single cases with no connection between them.
An outbreak is defined against what is expected here, not against zero. Two cases can be an outbreak.
